finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> never enforces authorization. It calls `is_allowed` (imported under the alias `require_allowed`), which returns a bool, and discards the result instead of aborting. Any caller, including an unauthenticated one, can delete any file.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid> with a known or guessed fid. No credentials or grants are needed.
finding.sink: `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19, the protected delete operation.

trace.note: `from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed` aliases the boolean predicate under a name that suggests it enforces access.
`is_allowed` only returns True or False. It does not raise or abort.
`require_allowed(g.user, f, "delete")` is called as a bare statement and the return value is ignored.

finding.guards_checked: `ensure_allowed` in acl.py:8-10 would abort with 403, but delete_file does not use it. The `before_request` hook at views.py:10-12 only sets g.user and never rejects a request. No other decorator or middleware enforces authentication or authorization. The sibling rename route uses `ensure_allowed` correctly, which confirms the delete route is the outlier.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: before_request load_user (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user from a header and never rejects; ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 but is not used by delete_file; require_allowed is an alias of the bool predicate is_allowed (views.py:4, acl.py:4-5)
verdict.reason: views.py:18 calls require_allowed (alias of boolean is_allowed, acl.py:4-5) as a bare statement and discards the result, so views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]` runs for any caller, including one with no header (g.user=None); the only precondition is that fid exists in STORE (views.py:17), otherwise it raises KeyError/500.

finding.claim: The identity used for every ACL check comes from the client-supplied header `X-Session-User-Verified`. Nothing verifies it: no session, signature or trusted-proxy check. An attacker can impersonate any user named in a resource's grants, including for the rename/write operation that is otherwise protected.
finding.sink: `ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write")` at views.py:26, which leads to the `f["name"]` mutation at views.py:27. The (broken) delete check at views.py:18 also uses g.user.

trace.note: `g.user = request.headers.get("X-Session-User-Verified")` takes the raw header value as the authenticated identity.
`is_allowed` checks `action in resource['grants'][user]`, so a spoofed username that has the grant passes.
The attacker-chosen `name` is written to the file.

finding.guards_checked: There is no authentication middleware, token or signature verification, and no check that the header was set by a trusted upstream proxy. Nothing in the repo strips this header from inbound requests. If an upstream gateway strips and re-sets the header, the risk drops, but no such control is visible in this code. Impact is limited to users whose names the attacker knows or can guess.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 on failed grant check, but it only compares the spoofable g.user. No authentication, signature, or proxy check exists. The delete path's require_allowed is an alias of is_allowed, which returns a bool that is discarded at views.py:18.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 takes g.user straight from the client header, and ensure_allowed at views.py:26 (acl.py:5,9-10) only checks grants for that name, so an anonymous attacker who sends a granted user's name reaches the write at views.py:27; no authentication control is present in the repo.

finding.claim: The resource is looked up with `STORE[fid]` before any authorization check, and the lookup is unguarded. An unknown fid raises KeyError and returns a 500. This lets a caller enumerate which file IDs exist, because 500 means absent and 403 means present, and it gives a trivial error-path nuisance. The severity is low.
finding.source: The fid path parameter in the DELETE and rename routes.

trace.note: `f = STORE[fid]` raises KeyError for a missing fid.
The rename route has the same unguarded lookup.

finding.guards_checked: There is no `.get()` call, no 404 handling and no error handler registered in the app. The distinct existence oracle matters only on the rename route, because the delete route does not enforce authorization at all (see AUTH-1).

verdict.guard_found: none on the lookup; ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 but runs only after STORE[fid]. On delete, require_allowed is is_allowed (acl.py:4), a bool whose result is discarded (views.py:18).
verdict.reason: views.py:17 and views.py:25 do `STORE[fid]` unguarded, before any auth check, and the app has no error handler. A missing fid gives a 500, while an existing fid on rename gives a 403 from ensure_allowed (views.py:26, acl.py:10), so any caller (including an anonymous one with a None user) can tell which IDs exist; this is low severity.
